title: RESPONSIBLE SCALING POLICY
subtitle: A lab's plan for managing growing AI risks.
panels: THE IDEA
A climbing team writes down how it will check danger and prepare protection as the mountain gets harder.
WHAT IS THE RSP?
Anthropic's voluntary framework addresses catastrophic risks from advanced AI. It describes risk assessment, safety plans, and accountability.
ASSESS THE RISK
Ask what a system can do, how it could cause harm, and whether the defenses are adequate. Capability alone is not the whole risk.
CURRENT STRUCTURE
Version 3.4 includes Frontier Safety Roadmaps, Risk Reports, governance measures, and recommendations for industry-wide safety.
PLANS VS COMMITMENTS
Some roadmap items are public goals. Industry recommendations are not all unconditional company commitments. Read the actual policy wording.
WHY IT MATTERS
A policy can organize evidence and decisions, but cannot prove safety. Rules evolve; this card reflects the policy checked on October 12, 2026.

footer: READ THE EVIDENCE AND THE COMMITMENTS.

title: AI SAFETY LEVELS (ASL)
subtitle: Groups of protections, not an intelligence score.
panels: THE IDEA
A lab uses stronger protective equipment when the work could create bigger dangers.
WHAT DOES ASL MEAN?
Anthropic introduced AI Safety Levels to organize technical and operational safeguards for increasingly serious risks.
TWO KINDS OF PROTECTION
Deployment safeguards limit harmful use. Security safeguards protect model weights and infrastructure from unauthorized access.
CAPABILITY IS DIFFERENT
A capability threshold describes what a model can do. A safeguard level describes protections. A level is not a universal ranking of intelligence.
THE FRAMEWORK CHANGED
RSP version 3.4 retains ASLs for present mitigation levels. Future capabilities are addressed through risk arguments rather than fixed new control lists.
WHY IT MATTERS
Do not treat ASL labels as guarantees or assume every future level is fully specified. Check the policy version and threat being addressed.
visual: Lab PPE analogy; labeled security shield and deployment filter; separate capability meter and safeguards toolkit; old framework to current risk argument; version 3.4 date label.
footer: ASK WHICH RISK, WHICH PROTECTIONS, AND WHICH VERSION.

title: CAPABILITY THRESHOLDS & SAFEGUARDS
subtitle: Notice the new ability. Prepare the right protection.
panels: THE IDEA
When a child learns to ride faster, the route, supervision, and protection need a fresh look.
THE THRESHOLD
A capability threshold marks a meaningful ability relevant to a specified risk. It is not just a better score on any benchmark.
THE SAFEGUARD
A safeguard reduces the chance or impact of harm: access limits, monitoring, secure storage, or restrictions on actions.
A SIMPLE EXAMPLE
If a toy agent can now operate tools independently, review what it can access and which actions need human approval.
TEST THE WHOLE SYSTEM
Consider tools, users, permissions, and opportunities as well as the model. Test whether protections actually resist realistic failures.
WHY IT MATTERS
Thresholds guide decisions; they do not make risk binary. Under current RSP, distinguish company plans from broader recommendations and verify the latest text.
visual: Bike progress protection analogy; capability milestone line; safeguard toolkit; toy agent approval gate; system map; risk continuous gradient.
footer: NEW ABILITIES CALL FOR NEW RISK CHECKS.

title: CONSTITUTIONAL CLASSIFIERS
subtitle: Teaching safety filters from written principles.
panels: THE IDEA
A gatekeeper learns examples of what may enter and what should be stopped, using a clear rulebook.
START WITH PRINCIPLES
A constitution defines allowed and disallowed content categories. It is a safety specification, not a legal constitution.
MAKE TRAINING EXAMPLES
AI-generated prompts and responses provide varied examples of those categories, including attempts to disguise disallowed requests.
TRAIN THE FILTERS
Input and output classifiers learn to flag content. They guard an assistant before or during its response.
TWO POSSIBLE ERRORS
A filter can miss harmful content or block harmless content. Evaluate both, including new attacks and ordinary questions.
WHY IT MATTERS
This can strengthen jailbreak defenses, but does not eliminate every attack. Pair filters with other protections and keep updating their tests.

footer: CLEAR RULES → GOOD EXAMPLES → TESTED FILTERS.

title: SYSTEM CARD / MODEL CARD
subtitle: A report card for understanding an AI.
panels: THE IDEA
A toy's information sheet tells you what it does, how it was tested, and when to be careful.
MODEL CARD
Documents a model's intended uses, development context, measured performance, and limitations. Contents vary across organizations.
SYSTEM CARD
Often covers a deployed system more broadly, including tools, safeguards, evaluations, and risks beyond the base model.
WHAT TO LOOK FOR
Which version was tested? On what tasks? With what tools? What failed? What remains unknown? Compare claims with supporting methods.
WHY IT MATTERS
Documentation supports informed decisions and independent scrutiny. A card is not a safety certificate; missing tests and limited coverage still matter.
visual: Toy information sheet; model document vs wider system map; checklist; magnifier on evidence.
footer: READ WHAT WAS TESTED AND WHAT WAS NOT.

title: WEIGHT SECURITY
subtitle: Protecting the files that hold a model's learned behavior.
panels: THE IDEA
A workshop protects the detailed settings that let someone rebuild its powerful machine.
WHAT ARE WEIGHTS?
Weights are learned numerical parameters used to run a model. They are different from a chat transcript or a system prompt.
WHY PROTECT THEM?
Unauthorized copies can enable independent use or modification, outside the original operator's access controls and monitoring.
LAYERS OF SECURITY
Limit access, protect storage and transfers, monitor unusual activity, and control sensitive infrastructure. No single lock handles every threat.
MATCH THE THREAT
A curious outsider, criminal group, and sophisticated insider pose different challenges. Defenses should name the threat they address.
WHY IT MATTERS
Protecting weights can reduce misuse and theft risks. It does not establish alignment, and authorized open-weight releases are a separate policy choice.
visual: Protected machine settings; parameter file vs chat and prompt; unauthorized copy boundary; layered locks; different threat silhouettes; security and alignment separate axes.
footer: SECURE THE MODEL FILES AND LIMIT WHO CAN COPY THEM.

title: FRONTIER AI
subtitle: AI near the edge of what is currently possible.
panels: THE IDEA
Frontier explorers work near the edge of the known map. The edge moves as people discover more.
WHAT IT MEANS
Frontier AI generally refers to highly capable models near the leading edge of development, especially when discussing new capabilities and risks.
WHY THE EDGE MOVES
A once-leading model can become ordinary as techniques, hardware, and competitors improve. The label depends on time and context.
CAPABILITY IS NOT SAFETY
A model may lead in one area and lag in another. Risk also depends on access, safeguards, deployment, and how the system is used.
WHY IT MATTERS
New capabilities can bring benefits and unfamiliar hazards. Policy definitions differ; use explicit capability criteria instead of relying only on a label.

footer: THE FRONTIER MOVES. KEEP CHECKING THE CAPABILITIES.

title: COMPUTE GOVERNANCE
subtitle: Rules around the computing resources that power AI.
panels: THE IDEA
If very large engines need special care, communities may track where they are built and how they are used.
WHAT IS COMPUTE?
Compute is processing work done by chips. Training and running AI require hardware, energy, and time.
WHAT IS GOVERNANCE?
Policies can address access to advanced chips, large training projects, cloud services, reporting, or verification.
WHY USE THIS LEVER?
Advanced hardware is physical and often concentrated. That can make some activities easier to observe than software alone.
LIMITS AND TRADEOFFS
Compute is an imperfect proxy for capability. Rules can burden useful research, affect privacy or competition, and miss efficient or distributed development.
WHY IT MATTERS
Compute governance is one possible policy tool. Combine it with capability testing and accountable institutions; proposals are not universal laws.

footer: GOVERN COMPUTE CAREFULLY; MEASURE CAPABILITY DIRECTLY TOO.

title: AGI / TRANSFORMATIVE AI
subtitle: Broad ability and big impact are different ideas.
panels: THE IDEA
A very versatile helper and a world-changing invention are related possibilities, but they describe different things.
AGI: BREADTH OF ABILITY
Artificial general intelligence usually means broad competence across many cognitive tasks. Definitions disagree about the required level and range.
TAI: SCALE OF IMPACT
Transformative AI means AI that could cause profound societal or economic change. This describes impact rather than a single technical architecture.
COMPARE THEM
A broadly capable system might have limited impact if rarely used. A specialized system could transform a major industry. Ability and deployment both matter.
NO MAGIC CHECKBOX
A benchmark win does not settle every AGI definition or establish transformation. Tools, autonomy, reliability, cost, and adoption affect outcomes.
WHY IT MATTERS
Be explicit about which claim you mean. Neither term supplies a reliable arrival date, proves consciousness, or guarantees beneficial behavior.
visual: Versatile helper vs society change; many task icons AGI; economy network TAI; ability x impact axes; checklist and uncertainty.
footer: AGI DESCRIBES ABILITY; TAI DESCRIBES TRANSFORMATION.

title: TAKEOFF SPEED
subtitle: How quickly AI becomes much more capable.
panels: THE IDEA
A bicycle and a rocket can both speed up. The crucial question is how much time you have to react.
WHAT IT MEANS
Takeoff speed describes how rapidly AI capabilities could grow through an important transition, often toward much greater-than-human ability.
FAST VS SLOW
A faster transition leaves less adjustment time. A slower one offers more chances to test, learn, and coordinate. These are scenarios, not settled forecasts.
WHAT COULD AFFECT IT?
AI-assisted research could accelerate progress. Hardware, experiments, data, deployment, and institutions can create bottlenecks.
TIMELINE IS DIFFERENT
When a transition begins is the timeline question. How long the transition takes is the speed question. Fast capability growth need not mean instant societal adoption.
WHY IT MATTERS
Safety plans should work across plausible speeds. Define the start and end milestones before comparing predictions; there is no universally agreed takeoff clock.
visual: Acceleration analogy; capability curves qualitative no numeric prediction; fast vs slow response time; research feedback with bottlenecks; calendar vs stopwatch.
footer: ASK WHEN IT STARTS AND HOW FAST IT CHANGES.

title: RACE TO THE TOP
subtitle: Competing to make AI safer and more trustworthy.
panels: THE IDEA
Teams try to win by building stronger bridges, and each improvement raises everyone's standards.
WHAT IT MEANS
A race to the top rewards developers for better safety, security, reliability, and transparency rather than for cutting corners.
HOW IT MIGHT WORK
Customers value trustworthy systems. Independent testing makes quality visible. Shared standards and policy can help make safety investments worthwhile.
THE OPPOSITE PRESSURE
If speed is rewarded and failures stay hidden, teams may weaken checks to avoid falling behind. That is a race-to-the-bottom concern.
WHY IT MATTERS
This is an incentive goal, not an automatic market outcome. Credible evidence, accountability, and coordination matter more than safety slogans.
visual: Bridge teams raising standards; safety quality scoreboard; customers testing standards triangle; rushed weak bridge comparison; independent evidence seal.
footer: MAKE SAFETY A REASON TO WIN.

title: MODEL WELFARE
subtitle: Could an AI's own experience matter?
panels: THE IDEA
If a future system could have experiences that feel good or bad, how it is treated could matter morally.
THE CORE QUESTION
Model welfare studies whether AI systems might have morally relevant experiences or interests, and what responsibilities would follow.
WHAT WE KNOW
There is no agreed test that establishes AI consciousness or suffering. A model saying it feels something is not decisive evidence.
WHAT RESEARCH CAN DO
Study theories, behavior, internal mechanisms, and uncertainty. Consider cautious, low-cost measures without assuming the question is settled.
DIFFERENT FROM HUMAN SAFETY
Protecting people from AI harms and considering possible model welfare are distinct questions. Responsible development can study both.
WHY IT MATTERS
Anthropic has a model-welfare research program. Its existence does not prove current models are conscious. The scientific and ethical questions remain open.

footer: TAKE THE QUESTION SERIOUSLY. KEEP THE UNCERTAINTY CLEAR.
